name: Brute Force
description: Adversary repeatedly guesses passwords against a service such as SSH, RDP, VPN or web login, hoping one attempt succeeds.
detection: Bursts of failed password attempts or invalid user errors from one source, often many usernames, sometimes followed by an accepted login from the same source.
response: Block the source IP, enforce lockout and MFA, check whether any attempt succeeded and review that account, rotate its credentials.

name: Password Spraying
description: Adversary tries one or a few common passwords across many accounts to stay under lockout thresholds.
detection: Many different usernames each failing once or twice from the same source, spread over time, possibly followed by a single successful logon.
response: Block the source, reset passwords for accounts that succeeded, enable MFA, alert on failures across many accounts.

name: Credential Stuffing
description: Adversary replays username and password pairs leaked from other breaches against a login service.
detection: High volume of logins using real looking email style usernames from many IPs, low success rate, automated user agents.
response: Rate limit logins, require MFA, block abusive IP ranges, force resets for any accounts that succeeded.

name: Network Service Discovery
description: Adversary probes hosts for open ports and running services to map what can be attacked.
detection: One source connecting to many ports or hosts in a short time, mostly denied or reset connections, sequential port numbers, SYN packets with no follow up, internal sweeps of ports like 445 or 3389.
response: Block or rate limit the source, find out if it is an internal host, verify which services are exposed, add scan detection.

name: Active Scanning
description: External adversary scans internet facing addresses and applications to find weaknesses before an attack.
detection: Probing requests across address ranges, vulnerability scanner user agents, requests for many common paths returning 404.
response: Block scanning sources at the edge, review exposed services, patch what the scan could have reached.

name: Application Layer Protocol: DNS
description: Malware hides command and control or data inside DNS queries and responses.
detection: Very long random looking subdomains, high entropy labels, large volumes of TXT or NULL queries to one domain, regular beaconing intervals, one host producing thousands of unique subdomains.
response: Sinkhole the domain, isolate the querying host, capture DNS logs, find the process that makes the queries.

name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
description: Malware blends command and control traffic into normal looking HTTP or HTTPS requests.
detection: Regular periodic connections to rare domains, unusual user agents, small requests with larger responses, traffic to newly registered domains.
response: Block the domain or IP, inspect the host, review proxy logs for the same beacon pattern.

name: Protocol Tunneling
description: Adversary wraps one protocol inside another, for example over DNS, ICMP, SSH or HTTPS, to evade controls.
detection: ICMP packets with large payloads, long lived SSH sessions with steady traffic, protocol mismatch on a port, DNS carrying non DNS data.
response: Block or inspect the tunnel endpoint, restrict unusual egress, isolate the source host if compromise is likely.

name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
description: Stolen data is sent out through the same channel the malware uses for command and control.
detection: Large outbound transfer to a rare external IP, bytes out far greater than bytes in, off hours uploads, long lived connections on odd ports, a server sending data it normally never sends.
response: Isolate the host, block the destination, identify what data was touched, preserve traffic captures, notify the data owner and incident lead.

name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
description: Data is sent out through a protocol that is not the normal command channel, such as FTP, DNS, ICMP or SMTP.
detection: Unexpected FTP or SMTP uploads, unusually large ICMP or DNS payloads, outbound transfers to personal storage or unknown hosts.
response: Block the protocol to that destination, isolate the host, measure what left, review data loss prevention alerts.

name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
description: Adversary attacks an internet facing app, for example with SQL injection, path traversal or remote code execution payloads.
detection: Web requests containing union select, or 1=1, ../ sequences, shell commands or unusual parameters, followed by 200 responses or 500 errors, then new outbound connections from the server.
response: Block the source at the web application firewall, patch or virtually patch, check for successful access and webshells.

name: Network Denial of Service
description: Adversary floods a network or service so legitimate users cannot reach it.
detection: Sudden surge of SYN or UDP packets from many sources to one service, connection table exhaustion, dropped packets, saturated bandwidth.
response: Enable rate limiting and SYN protection, use upstream scrubbing, block abusive ranges, scale capacity, notify the provider.

name: Endpoint Denial of Service
description: Adversary exhausts the resources of a specific server or application, for example with slow requests or heavy queries.
detection: Spike of requests to one endpoint, many slow connections held open, rising CPU or memory with normal network volume.
response: Rate limit the endpoint, block abusive clients, add timeouts, scale the service.

name: Remote Services: SSH
description: Adversary uses valid credentials or keys to move between hosts over SSH.
detection: One host opening SSH sessions to many internal hosts in a short time, the same key used widely, SSH from servers that normally never initiate it.
response: Identify the source account and key, disable or rotate them, isolate the originating host, review bastion policy.

name: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
description: Adversary logs in to other systems over RDP using valid accounts.
detection: RDP logons from unusual sources or at unusual hours, RDP from servers to workstations, many failed logons then a success.
response: Restrict RDP to a jump host, enforce MFA, disable the account if misuse is confirmed, review the source host.

name: Valid Accounts
description: Adversary uses legitimate credentials they have stolen or guessed, making activity look normal.
detection: Logins from new locations or devices, impossible travel, successful login right after many failures, use of accounts outside working hours.
response: Reset credentials, end active sessions, require MFA, review what the account accessed.

name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
description: Adversary sits between two parties, for example by ARP or DNS spoofing, to read or change traffic.
detection: Duplicate IP to MAC mappings, ARP replies nobody asked for, sudden gateway MAC change, certificate warnings for internal sites.
response: Isolate the spoofing host or port, enable dynamic ARP inspection, verify gateway address, review captured sessions.

name: Network Sniffing
description: Adversary captures network traffic to collect credentials and other data in transit.
detection: Network interface in promiscuous mode, packet capture tools on hosts, switch mirror ports enabled unexpectedly.
response: Remove the capture tool or port mirror, isolate the host, use encrypted protocols, rotate credentials that crossed the network.

name: Dynamic Resolution
description: Malware generates or changes domains on the fly so its infrastructure is hard to block.
detection: Many queries for random looking domains that mostly return NXDOMAIN, domain names that look algorithmically generated, fast changing resolved IPs.
response: Block the generated domain pattern, isolate the querying host, find the process responsible.

name: External Remote Services
description: Adversary enters the network through exposed remote access such as VPN, RDP gateways or remote admin tools.
detection: Logins to VPN or remote gateways from unusual countries, service accounts used remotely, sudden use of dormant remote access accounts.
response: Require MFA on remote access, geo restrict, disable unused accounts, review session history.
